dossier.understanding: Authentication in Requests is applied through a flexible callable interface: an auth parameter (either a tuple for basic auth, an AuthBase subclass, or any callable) is passed through the request preparation flow and invoked on a PreparedRequest to inject credentials. For synchronous authentication (HTTPBasicAuth), this happens once during preparation by adding an Authorization header. For challenge-response authentication (HTTPDigestAuth), it registers a response hook that watches for 401 responses, extracts authentication challenges, and automatically retries the request with a computed Digest header. The authentication system integrates with the Session's credential merging and with netrc file support.

contracts.contract: An auth handler must be callable, accepting a PreparedRequest and returning a modified PreparedRequest. Signature: __call__(self, r: PreparedRequest) -> PreparedRequest. The handler must update r in-place or return a new PreparedRequest; commonly modifies r.headers to add authentication. See HTTPBasicAuth.__call__ and HTTPDigestAuth.__call__ for examples.

Takes an AuthType parameter that can be (1) a 2-tuple (username, password) automatically converted to HTTPBasicAuth, (2) an AuthBase subclass or callable accepting PreparedRequest and returning PreparedRequest, or (3) None for no auth. Callables receive the fully-prepared request so they can make auth decisions based on full context.

evidence_refs.clarifies: HTTPBasicAuth and HTTPDigestAuth are the two standard auth implementations. HTTPBasicAuth injects a single Authorization header. HTTPDigestAuth registers response hooks for challenge handling. Both implement AuthBase.__call__ contract.
PreparedRequest.prepare_auth is where auth is actually applied. It shows the tuple-to-HTTPBasicAuth conversion and the auth handler invocation pattern.

Session.prepare_request shows how request-level and session-level auth are merged. Session.request is the user-facing entry point. Session.send dispatches response hooks where auth challenges are handled.
Module-level convenience functions (get, post, etc.) create temporary Sessions and delegate to Session.request, showing the flow for single-request authentication.

context: Authentication in Requests is fundamentally pluggable: any callable that modifies a PreparedRequest can serve as an auth handler. The library provides HTTPBasicAuth and HTTPDigestAuth as standard implementations, but users can implement custom auth (OAuth, NTLM, etc.) by subclassing AuthBase or providing any callable.

The two-phase application of auth reflects HTTP reality: basic auth is pre-computed and sent with every request, while digest auth requires a server challenge (401 response) to compute credentials. Requests handles both transparently by using hooks for the challenge-response case.

Auth is applied last during request preparation (lines 445-446 comment in models.py: 'prepare_auth must be last to enable authentication schemes such as OAuth'). This is crucial because OAuth and similar schemes need the full prepared request (URL, method, body, headers) to compute their signatures.

Session-level auth allows credentials to be set once and applied to all requests made through that session, reducing boilerplate. Request-level auth always takes precedence, allowing per-request credential override.

The netrc integration (lines 537-538 in sessions.py) provides automatic credential loading from ~/.netrc files when trust_env=True, enabling seamless authentication without explicit credentials in code.
HTTPDigestAuth's per-thread state management (threading.local at line 145 in auth.py) ensures that nonce counting and challenge caching work correctly in multithreaded environments.
Digest auth's handle_401 hook limits retries to once (num_401_calls < 2) to prevent infinite retry loops if the server keeps rejecting credentials.

learning_path.title: Learn the auth callable contract that everything builds on
learning_path.why: Every part of the auth system assumes this contract; understanding it first makes every downstream node immediately legible
learning_path.understand: An auth handler is any callable that accepts a PreparedRequest and returns a modified PreparedRequest — AuthBase formalises this as a single __call__ signature, making auth handlers interchangeable with plain functions or lambdas

learning_path.title: See the simplest auth implementation: HTTPBasicAuth
learning_path.why: HTTPBasicAuth is the canonical one-liner that shows exactly what an auth handler must do: mutate the PreparedRequest's headers and return it
learning_path.understand: Basic auth fulfils the contract by computing a base64-encoded Authorization header in a single step — receiving a PreparedRequest and returning it modified, with no need for any server interaction

learning_path.title: Trace how auth enters and flows through Session.request
learning_path.why: This is the public API surface where auth is first accepted; understanding it places all subsequent steps in context
learning_path.understand: Session.request accepts auth as a tuple or callable, wraps it in a Request object, and delegates immediately to prepare_request — the auth value is not touched here, just carried forward

learning_path.title: Understand how session-level and request-level auth are merged
learning_path.why: Auth can come from two places simultaneously; knowing the precedence rule is essential before reading prepare_request
learning_path.understand: For non-dict values like auth callables, merge_setting returns the request-level value when present and falls back to the session-level value — request auth always wins, enabling per-request credential overrides

learning_path.title: See where netrc fallback and merge happen in Session.prepare_request
learning_path.why: This is where the three auth sources — request, session, and netrc — are resolved into a single value before preparation
learning_path.understand: prepare_request applies the auth cascade: request auth beats session auth (via merge_setting), and netrc credentials are injected only when both are absent and trust_env is True — the resolved auth is then passed to PreparedRequest.prepare

learning_path.title: Understand why auth is invoked last in the preparation pipeline
learning_path.why: The ordering of prepare steps is a deliberate design constraint that auth implementers must respect
learning_path.understand: prepare_auth is the final preparation step by design — auth handlers receive a fully-built PreparedRequest (URL, method, headers, body all set) so they can compute signatures over the complete request, which is required for schemes like OAuth

learning_path.title: Examine where the auth callable is actually invoked on the request
learning_path.why: This is the precise call site where any auth handler — basic, digest, or custom — modifies the request
learning_path.understand: prepare_auth normalises a 2-tuple to HTTPBasicAuth, then calls auth_handler(self) on the fully-prepared request; it updates the PreparedRequest in place from the returned object and recomputes Content-Length, accommodating auth handlers that change the body

learning_path.title: Learn how HTTPDigestAuth registers hooks for challenge-response auth
learning_path.why: Digest auth introduces a two-phase pattern that is fundamentally different from basic auth and requires understanding hooks
learning_path.understand: HTTPDigestAuth.__call__ optionally pre-fills the Authorization header from a cached nonce, then registers handle_401 and handle_redirect as response hooks — the real credential computation is deferred until a 401 arrives, demonstrating the challenge-response pattern inside the same callable contract

learning_path.title: See how response hooks are registered on a PreparedRequest
learning_path.why: Digest auth's challenge-response behaviour depends on this mechanism; understanding it explains how a hook registered during preparation can act on the live response
learning_path.understand: register_hook appends a callable to the named event list on the PreparedRequest's hooks dict; callables registered here persist through transmission and are dispatched by Session.send after the response arrives

learning_path.title: Follow how Session.send fires response hooks including auth handlers
learning_path.why: Session.send is where the digest auth cycle closes — the adapter sends the request and hooks on the response run handle_401
learning_path.understand: After the adapter returns a response, Session.send calls dispatch_hook('response', ...) which invokes every registered response hook in order; the return value of each hook replaces the response, so handle_401 can transparently substitute a retried response for the original 401

learning_path.title: Understand how dispatch_hook invokes auth callbacks
learning_path.why: dispatch_hook is the glue between Session.send and every registered hook including handle_401
learning_path.understand: dispatch_hook iterates the hook list for a given event and replaces the data with each hook's non-None return value — this chained replacement is why handle_401 can return a completely new response that Session.send treats as the authoritative result

learning_path.title: Trace the full digest challenge-response retry inside handle_401
learning_path.why: This is the most complex part of the auth system — it shows request rewriting, body position rewinding, cookie propagation, and retry limiting all working together
learning_path.understand: handle_401 parses the WWW-Authenticate challenge, copies the original PreparedRequest, injects a freshly computed Digest Authorization header, and resends it directly via r.connection.send — the retry is limited to one attempt (num_401_calls < 2) to prevent infinite loops, and the original 401 is appended to history

dossier.understanding: FastAPI's dependency injection system is a declarative mechanism that allows endpoint functions and other dependencies to declare their parameter requirements through function signatures and annotations. At the core is the Dependant model—a hierarchical structure that analyzes and stores metadata about a function's parameters, distinguishing between direct request data (path/query/header/cookie/body params), other dependencies (via Depends/Security), and special-case parameters (Request, Response, BackgroundTasks, etc.). During route registration, get_dependant recursively analyzes the endpoint function's signature to build a dependency tree. At request time, solve_dependencies asynchronously resolves this entire tree by recursively calling dependencies, extracting values from the request (path params, query params, etc.), executing dependency callables (with async/sync/generator support), and caching results to avoid duplicate calls. The system supports advanced features like dependency overrides (for testing), scoped caching, generator-based context managers (for resource lifecycle), and OAuth2 security scopes.

Stores lists of path/query/header/cookie/body parameters, nested dependencies, caching configuration, and callable reference. If the parameter is a Depends/Security, recursively calls get_dependant on the dependency callable (line 334-342), creating a tree. If it's a request parameter, creates a ModelField and stores it in the appropriate list (path_params, query_params, etc.).
For special types like Request or Response, records the parameter name in the Dependant so they can be injected later.
Returns the fully built Dependant tree. Route stores it as self.dependant for use at request time.

Returns a SolvedDependency containing the collected values dict, any validation errors, background tasks, response object, and the filled dependency cache.

contracts.contract: A Dependant is a tree node representing a function's dependencies and parameters. Must store lists of path_params, query_params, header_params, cookie_params, body_params (ModelField lists), a dependencies list (sub-Dependants), special parameter names (request_param_name, response_param_name, etc.), and a callable. Must provide cache_key, oauth_scopes, and methods to determine if the callable is async/generator/etc. Serves as the contract between analysis (get_dependant) and resolution (solve_dependencies).

Given a parameter name, annotation, default value, and whether it's a path param, returns a ParamDetails indicating: (1) type_annotation—the underlying type; (2) depends—a Depends/Security object if the parameter is a dependency, or None; (3) field—a ModelField if the parameter is a request param, or None. Only one of depends or field should be non-None. Used by get_dependant to classify each parameter.

Async function that recursively resolves a Dependant tree for a given request. Takes a Request/WebSocket, a Dependant tree, optional body, response, background_tasks, dependency_overrides_provider, dependency_cache, and embed_body_fields. Returns a SolvedDependency containing: values dict (parameter name → resolved value), errors list, background_tasks, response object, and updated dependency_cache. Must handle async/sync/generator callables, extract request parameters, inject special types, and apply caching.

User-facing class holding a dependency callable, use_cache flag, and optional scope. When used as a parameter annotation (e.g., param: int = Depends(some_func)), signals to FastAPI that the parameter should be resolved by calling some_func. Instances are immutable and used as markers during signature analysis.

prerequisites.concept: Function signatures and annotations in Python
prerequisites.why_needed: The DI system works by inspecting function signatures and type annotations to determine what dependencies and parameters are needed. Understanding inspect.signature and typing.Annotated is essential.
The system differentiates between sync and async dependencies and executes them appropriately. Understanding how to check if a function is a coroutine and how to await is essential.
FastAPI supports dependencies that are generators (with yield) for setup/teardown logic. Understanding context managers and generator mechanics is needed to understand _solve_generator.
The dependency cache uses a dict keyed by cache_key tuples. Understanding how to use dicts as caches and cache key computation is important.

prerequisites.concept: Recursive data structures and tree traversal
prerequisites.why_needed: The Dependant structure is recursive (dependencies list contains sub-Dependants). Both get_dependant and solve_dependencies traverse this tree recursively.
Request parameters are represented as ModelField objects that handle validation and serialization. Understanding what ModelField is helps understand how query/path/body params are represented.
The DI system integrates with ASGI by receiving Request/WebSocket objects and returning Response objects. Understanding basic ASGI concepts helps understand the request/response flow.

evidence_refs.clarifies: Shows practical dependency injection usage. Demonstrates that dependencies are cached within a request (test_sub_counter shows dep_counter called once when referenced twice), but without cache when use_cache=False (test_sub_counter_no_cache). Security with scopes creates separate cache entries (test_security_cache).

context: The DI system is split into two phases: analysis (get_dependant, called at route registration) and resolution (solve_dependencies, called at request time). This separation allows FastAPI to build the dependency graph once and reuse it for many requests.

Caching is per-request, not global. The same dependency function called twice in the same request returns the same value (same cache_key), but different requests start with an empty cache. This is done via the dependency_cache dict passed through solve_dependencies recursively.

The system supports dependency overrides for testing via dependency_overrides_provider (typically the FastAPI app instance). When a dependency is overridden, solve_dependencies re-analyzes the override callable with get_dependant.
Generator dependencies are wrapped as context managers and entered into an AsyncExitStack so cleanup code (after yield) runs when the request finishes or the request-scoped AsyncExitStack exits.

Special parameters like Request, Response, BackgroundTasks, and SecurityScopes are injected directly without requiring user code—add_non_field_param_to_dependency detects their types and records their names in the Dependant.
OAuth2 Security dependencies can have scopes that affect caching. Dependencies with different scopes have different cache keys even if the callable is the same.

open_questions.question: Exactly how does AsyncExitStack scope work between function-scoped and request-scoped dependencies? The code references both fastapi_inner_astack (request-scoped) and fastapi_function_astack (function-scoped) but the setup of these stacks was not traced.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Understanding lifecycle management and cleanup order is important for advanced use cases with nested dependencies that have different scopes.

open_questions.question: How does dependency_overrides_provider.dependency_overrides get populated? The code checks for overrides but the mechanism for setting them was not investigated.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Understanding how to use dependency overrides for testing is a practical feature users need to know about, but the configuration mechanism was not fully traced.

learning_path.title: Learn the public API: Depends and Security
learning_path.why: These are the annotations users write to declare dependencies, so understanding their fields is the entry point to the whole system.
learning_path.understand: Depends wraps a callable plus two flags (use_cache, scope) that control caching and lifecycle; Security extends it with OAuth2 scopes, and those three fields drive nearly every downstream decision.

learning_path.title: Understand the Dependant data model
learning_path.why: Every phase of the DI system—analysis, resolution, caching—reads from or writes to this structure, so its fields define what information the system tracks.
learning_path.understand: Dependant is a recursive tree node that partitions a function's parameters into typed lists (path/query/header/cookie/body params, sub-Dependants) plus special-injection slots and a callable reference; the tree is built once at registration and traversed on every request.

learning_path.title: See how cache_key makes per-request deduplication work
learning_path.why: Caching is one of the most misunderstood DI behaviours; understanding the key reveals exactly when two references to the same dependency are collapsed into one call.
learning_path.understand: cache_key is a tuple of (callable, sorted-oauth-scopes, scope-string), so two Depends annotations sharing a callable are deduplicated unless they differ by Security scopes or dependency scope; this key is used both for lookup and storage inside the per-request dependency_cache dict.

learning_path.title: Trace parameter classification in analyze_param
learning_path.why: This is where each function parameter is sorted into one of three buckets—dependency, request field, or special type—which determines how it will be handled in every later phase.
learning_path.understand: analyze_param unwraps Annotated, then returns a ParamDetails where exactly one of (depends, field) is set: depends for Depends/Security annotations (from either Annotated metadata or a default value), a ModelField for Query/Path/Body etc., and neither for special built-in types like Request or Response.

learning_path.title: See how special built-in injections are recorded
learning_path.why: Knowing that Request, Response, BackgroundTasks, and SecurityScopes are injected without Depends clarifies the full set of things FastAPI can inject.
learning_path.understand: add_non_field_param_to_dependency detects framework types by subclass check and writes the parameter name into the matching slot on Dependant (e.g., request_param_name); at resolve time, solve_dependencies reads those slots to inject live request objects directly—no user-written callable involved.

learning_path.title: Follow dependency tree construction in get_dependant
learning_path.why: This is the analysis phase that converts a raw function signature into the Dependant tree the rest of the system consumes.
learning_path.understand: get_dependant iterates the function's typed signature, calls analyze_param for each parameter, then either recurses into get_dependant for Depends parameters (appending sub-Dependants to dependencies), delegates to add_non_field_param_to_dependency for special types, or appends a ModelField to the appropriate param list—making the tree construction fully recursive and self-similar.

learning_path.title: See how route registration wires get_dependant into APIRoute
learning_path.why: This is the moment the Dependant tree is actually built and stored, separating the analysis phase from request-time resolution.
learning_path.understand: During route registration, APIRoute.__init__ calls get_dependant on the endpoint and calls get_parameterless_sub_dependant for each entry in the route-level dependencies list, appending all resulting sub-Dependants into the endpoint Dependant's dependencies; the completed tree is stored as self.dependant and reused for every subsequent request.

learning_path.title: Understand generator dependencies and lifecycle management
learning_path.why: Generator-based dependencies (yield-style setup/teardown) are a widely used pattern; understanding how they're wrapped explains why cleanup code runs reliably after the request ends.
learning_path.understand: _solve_generator wraps the generator callable in contextmanager (or asynccontextmanager) and enters the resulting context manager into the appropriate AsyncExitStack, so the code after yield executes when the stack exits—request-scoped generators use the inner request stack while function-scoped generators use the per-call function stack. Note: the exact setup and exit ordering of these two stacks was not fully traced in the investigation.

learning_path.title: Walk through full runtime resolution in solve_dependencies
learning_path.why: This is the execution engine of the DI system; tracing it reveals how all earlier concepts—the tree, caching, overrides, generator lifecycle, and special injections—come together for each request.
learning_path.understand: solve_dependencies recurses depth-first through dependant.dependencies, applying overrides (by re-running get_dependant on the replacement callable), checking the per-request cache before each call, dispatching to _solve_generator for yield-based deps or awaiting/threadpool-running regular callables, then extracts request params and injects special framework types, finally returning a SolvedDependency whose values dict is passed as **kwargs to the endpoint.

learning_path.title: See the complete request lifecycle in get_request_handler
learning_path.why: This is the outermost integration point that ties body parsing, dependency resolution, endpoint invocation, and response serialization into the single ASGI callable FastAPI exposes per route.
learning_path.understand: get_request_handler closes over the pre-built Dependant tree and returns an async ASGI app that, per request, parses the body, calls solve_dependencies to obtain the resolved values dict, calls the endpoint with **solved_result.values, and serializes the return value—making the two-phase design (analysis at registration, resolution at runtime) concrete and complete.
